p: On the fifteenth of June, twelve hundred and fifteen, in a meadow beside the Thames called Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, King John of England set his seal to a document drawn up by his rebellious barons. It was written in Latin, and it is known by its Latin name, Magna Carta, which means simply the Great Charter. It was meant to end a civil war. It failed: within three months the pope, at the king's request, had annulled it, and the war began again. And yet it has become the most famous document in English history, and, the Encyclopaedia tells me, one of the most famous in the world, invoked by the founders of the United States, by the authors of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights after the Second World War, and by prisoners and reformers in many lands. How a failed peace treaty became a sacred text is one of the most interesting stories in the history of ideas.

John was the youngest son of Henry the Second and Eleanor of Aquitaine, and the brother of Richard the Lionheart, whom he succeeded in eleven ninety-nine. He has the worst reputation of any English king. Some of it he deserved. He very probably had his young nephew Arthur, who had a better claim to the throne, murdered. He lost almost all his family's lands in France, including Normandy, to the French king Philip Augustus, by twelve hundred and four, and so earned the nickname Lackland, or later, Softsword. He quarrelled with the pope over the appointment of an Archbishop of Canterbury, and England lay for years under an interdict, during which no church services could be held, until John submitted and made England a fief of the papacy. To pay for his wars and his efforts to recover his French lands, he squeezed his barons mercilessly, by every means the feudal law allowed and many it did not: heavy fines, arbitrary seizures of land, the sale of rich widows in marriage, the holding of the sons of his barons as hostages. When his great expedition to recover his French lands ended in defeat at the battle of Bouvines in twelve fourteen, the barons rebelled and took London.

The charter has some sixty clauses, most of them concerned with the particular grievances of the barons, and very dull reading: the payments due when an heir inherits his land, the rights of widows, the debts owed to Jews, the removal of fish-weirs from the Thames, the dismissal of certain foreign officials by name. But two clauses have outlived all the rest. The thirty-ninth declares that no free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or in any way ruined, nor will the king proceed against him or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land. The fortieth declares: to no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay, right or justice.

There was also a clause, the sixty-first, establishing a council of twenty-five barons who might, if the king broke the charter, make war upon him to compel him to keep it. It is hardly surprising that John sought to escape it. No king could accept such a thing and remain a king.

John died of dysentery in October twelve sixteen, having lost, by an often repeated story, his baggage train with his treasure in the quicksands of the Wash. His heir, Henry the Third, was a boy of nine, and his regents, to win back the rebel barons, reissued the charter in a revised form, without the clause of the twenty-five. It was reissued again in twelve seventeen and twelve twenty-five, and confirmed by later kings many times. It became a part of the law of England, read aloud in the county courts, and its principle that the king himself is bound by the law entered the common understanding of the nation.

Its greatest revival came in the seventeenth century, in the struggle between Parliament and the Stuart kings. Sir Edward Coke, the great lawyer and Chief Justice, interpreted the charter, with more patriotism than historical accuracy, as a guarantee of the ancient liberties of all Englishmen, including trial by jury and the writ of habeas corpus, a Latin phrase meaning you shall have the body, by which a judge can order a jailer to bring a prisoner before the court and show by what right he is held. The barons of twelve fifteen had thought of none of these things. But Coke's misreading became the reading. The charter was carried by the colonists to America, and the founders of the American republic, in their quarrel with the British Crown, appealed to it as fervently as Coke had done.

The historian must say plainly that Magna Carta was a charter of privileges for a class of great landowners, extracted by force from a weak king, and that most Englishmen of the thirteenth century, who were unfree peasants, gained little or nothing from it. The free men of clause thirty-nine were a minority. Yet that is not the whole truth. For the charter established, in writing, a principle more powerful than its authors understood: that there is a law of the land which binds the king, and that a government which acts outside that law is a tyranny. Once written, that principle could be read by each generation in a wider sense. It is the nature of great words to grow larger than the men who wrote them. Four copies of the charter of twelve fifteen survive. I have seen the two in the British Museum. They are small, faded, and in a cramped hand. They do not look like the foundation of anything.
